messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Tax Inspector
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 35

**Case Vignette: "Khalid"**

Khalid is a 30-year-old tax inspector who presents with a guarded, almost meticulous demeanor. He arrives for sessions directly from work, still wearing a pressed shirt and tie, and sits with his back to the wall, scanning the room before speaking. He is divorced and lives alone in a small apartment.

The traumatic event occurred fourteen months ago, on a rainy Tuesday evening. Khalid was driving home from a routine audit at a commercial warehouse. The road was slick, and visibility was poor. He remembers a single moment of clarity: the headlights of an oncoming pickup truck veering into his lane. He swerved hard, but his sedan hydroplaned, spun, and slammed driver-side-first into a concrete barrier. He was conscious throughout, pinned for nearly forty minutes while emergency services cut him free. He recalls the smell of gasoline, the sound of twisted metal being pried apart, and the paramedic’s voice telling him to stay awake. He sustained a fractured clavicle and three broken ribs, but no traumatic brain injury.

In the months following the accident, Khalid’s life began to contract. He stopped driving entirely for the first six weeks, relying on taxis and his then-wife for transport. The marriage, already strained by long work hours, dissolved within four months. His wife told him he was “not the same person” and that he seemed “paranoid and unreachable.” Khalid agrees with her assessment, but without blame. He describes feeling as though a pane of glass has been placed between himself and the world.

At work, Khalid performs his duties with robotic precision. He is known as a quiet, efficient inspector. But he now refuses to drive to any audit site that requires him to take a highway or a bridge. He has memorized surface-street routes for every location in his jurisdiction, adding forty-five minutes to his commute each way. He tells no one about this strategy. When a colleague offers him a ride to a joint inspection, Khalid declines, citing a “personal appointment.” The truth is the thought of being a passenger in a car is unbearable. He feels a surge of panic when the car reaches forty miles per hour, and he grips the door handle so hard his knuckles whiten. He has begun to dread the monthly team meetings because they require him to cross a major intersection where he once saw a minor fender bender.

At home, Khalid’s apartment is spotless and ordered. He sleeps only in the living room, on a recliner, because he cannot lie flat in a bed without feeling the phantom compression of the seatbelt against his chest. He wakes three to four times a night, often from a dream where he is still trapped in the car, the hydraulic cutters pressing closer to his face. He does not drink alcohol or use drugs; he simply endures. He has stopped calling friends. He no longer visits his mother, who lives an hour away, because the drive feels impossible.

The PCL-5 score of 35 reflects a moderate level of symptom severity. Khalid endorses moderate re-experiencing: intrusive images of the headlights appear when he sees rain on a windshield. He endorses avoidance: he has not driven on the highway since the crash. He endorses negative alterations in cognition and mood: he feels detached from others, and he struggles to remember details of the weeks immediately following the accident. He endorses marked alterations in arousal: he startles at the sound of a car horn, and he has a persistent sense of a foreshortened future. He tells me, quietly, that he does not expect to live past forty. He cannot explain why.

Khalid does not see himself as a trauma survivor. He sees himself as a man who was in a bad accident and who now has to be careful. He is not seeking relief from symptoms. He is seeking permission to stop feeling so alone.
